source: Corbett & Anderson (1995) Knowledge tracing: Modeling the acquisition of procedural knowledge
finding: Founding model. A two-state hidden Markov model per skill: learned or unlearned. Four parameters: prior p(L0), learning p(T), guess p(G), slip p(S). After each answer the tutor updates the chance the skill is learned, and the student moves on at a mastery threshold.
numbers: Mastery threshold usually 0.95 (from memory). Built on ACT-R production rules and the Lisp tutor. Fitted values and posttest correlations not checked this session.
limits: Paywalled, not opened; content from memory and from citing papers. Assumes one skill per step, no forgetting, one fixed parameter set for all learners.
agent_relevance: A per-subskill belief with a stop rule is the oldest template for knowing when a learner has it. Our agent could track a belief per sub-skill and stop practice on a threshold, not a feeling.

source: Anderson, Corbett, Koedinger & Pelletier (1995) Cognitive tutors: Lessons learned
finding: Reviews Lisp, geometry and algebra tutors built on ACT-R. Two core ideas: model tracing (check each step against an ideal rule model) and knowledge tracing (estimate mastery per rule).
numbers: Not verified this session. From memory: Lisp tutor students finished in roughly one third to one half less time with equal or better test scores; algebra pilot about one standard deviation on locally built tests.
limits: Early studies used author-built tests and small samples. Large later trials found smaller effects (see Pane line).
agent_relevance: Check each step with a rule model and give feedback at once. This maps onto our code-run checks: the check is plain code, not the model's opinion (G2).

source: Khajah, Lindsey & Mozer (2016) How deep is knowledge tracing?
finding: Re-ran DKT against BKT extended with forgetting, learner ability and skill discovery. Extended BKT matches DKT on average, so the win did not need depth. Piech's BKT AUC of 0.67 on Assistments looked too low; classic BKT scored 0.73 here.
numbers: Assistments: classic BKT AUC 0.73, BKT+F 0.83. Extended BKT vs DKT: +20.0% on Synthetic, +3.0% on Spanish, -8.3% (0.03 AUC) on Assistments, -3.5% (0.01) on Statics. Statics BKT+FSA 0.75 vs DKT 0.76. Spanish 0.846 vs 0.836. Synthetic BKT+S 0.80 vs DKT 0.75.
quote: knowledge tracing may be a domain that does not require 'depth'
limits: Khan Academy data was not available, so that set was not checked. Authors say exercise-indexed skill discovery could lift BKT further (Statics 0.81).
agent_relevance: Part of DKT's win came from weak baselines. Before crediting a learned component, test a strong plain baseline with the same features.

source: Piech et al. (2015) Deep Knowledge Tracing
finding: Fed student exercise-and-answer sequences to an LSTM that predicts the next answer. Claimed a big AUC lift over BKT with no hand-made skill labels.
numbers: AUC: Assistments marginal 0.62, BKT 0.67, best BKT in literature 0.69, DKT 0.86. Khan Math (47,495 students, 1.4M answers): marginal 0.63, BKT 0.68, DKT 0.85. Simulated-5 (4,000 students, 50 exercises): DKT 0.82. Authors claim 25% AUC gain over best prior result.
quote: A 25% gain in AUC over the best previous result on a knowledge tracing benchmark.
limits: 5-fold cross validation. Later work (Khajah 2016, Gervet 2020) found the gain shrinks with fair baselines. Khan data is not public.
agent_relevance: An unstructured sequence model beat expert skill tags but gave no readable state. Our schema keeps readable states (S0-S9) on purpose.

source: Piech et al. (2015) DKT exercise influence graph
finding: Defines influence J(j|i) as the net's predicted change in correctness on exercise j after exercise i was answered correctly. The graph recovers prerequisite links in simulated and Khan data.
numbers: Section 6.2 of the paper; no AUC attached to this step.
limits: Gervet 2020 shows KC-specific DKT with no cross-skill input still beats logistic on two sets, so not all of the gain is cross-skill.
agent_relevance: A learned dependency graph between tasks is an optional later feature for choosing the next task.

source: Gervet, Koedinger, Schneider & Mitchell (2020) When is deep learning the best approach to knowledge tracing?
finding: Nine real datasets, one pipeline. Logistic regression with good features leads on 4 sets (algebra05, bridge06, assistments09, spanish); DKT leads on 5 (assistments12, assistments17, statics, squirrel, assistments15). BKT lags. DKT wins on large data or when order and timing matter.
numbers: assistments17: DKT 0.770 vs best logistic 0.714 AUC (gap +0.056), but only +0.016 on first attempts. Other DKT gaps: +0.029 assistments15, +0.020 assistments12, +0.010 statics, +0.007 squirrel. algebra05: Best-LR 0.831, DKT 0.821.
quote: logistic regression with the right set of features leads on datasets of moderate size
limits: SAKT was below DKT on all nine. Could not reproduce the SAKT paper's AUC of 0.85 on ASSISTment 2015; got 0.73. Datasets are small by NLP standards.
agent_relevance: Deep gains are real but small and depend on data size and on using repeat attempts. Good simple features nearly close the gap.

source: Gervet et al. (2020) ablations
finding: DAS3H's boost over PFA comes from simple time-window features. A nonlinear net adds a bit on top, on some data only. KC features add little on most sets.
numbers: Feedforward net vs best logistic: +0.048 AUC on assistments17, +0.014 on assistments12. KC features add 0.01 AUC or less on most sets; about 0.03 on the KDD Cup sets (algebra05, bridge06).
limits: Same nine datasets; no human learning outcome measured.
agent_relevance: Order and recency carry real signal. Keep an ordered log of attempts, not just counts. Skill tags matter little on most data.

source: Pavlik, Eglington & Harrell-Williams (2021) Logistic Knowledge Tracing: a constrained framework for learner modeling
finding: Puts Performance Factors Analysis (PFA), recency and decay features, and per-student terms into one logistic family. Many 'different' tracers are feature choices in one model.
numbers: Reports McFadden R2, RMSE and AUC on Assistments and the Andes tutor (345,536 observations). Example test AUCs seen: 0.782 for a propdec-KC model, 0.749 for logsuc+logfail on another set.
limits: Not a head-to-head with DKT; the authors call that future work. Fits depend on the dataset and KC map.
agent_relevance: Interpretable features can be tested one at a time. A scaffold's state variables can be tested the same way: add one, measure held-out gain.

source: Metric caveat: how overall AUC is aggregated (Khajah 2016)
finding: Piech weighted every trial equally. Pardos and Heffernan averaged per-skill AUC. Per-skill averaging punishes skills with few trials and removes lift from telling skills apart.
numbers: Same Assistments data: BKT 0.67 (Piech), 0.69 (best per-skill average, Pardos), 0.73 (Khajah classic BKT), 0.83 (BKT+F).
limits: Which aggregation Piech used for DKT could not be checked.
agent_relevance: Re-run baselines under the same metric before claiming a win.

source: Khajah et al. (2016) interpretability argument
finding: BKT extensions keep meaning in their parameters (forgetting, ability, skill partition). DKT's internal state is hard to read.
numbers: A one-parameter recency model fit Assistments reliably. Forgetting did not help on Synthetic because simulated students never forget.
limits: Whether forgetting matters depends on the time gap between sessions.
agent_relevance: If our agent must explain why it moved on, a model with readable parameters beats a hidden state.

source: Language Model Can Do Knowledge Tracing (LKT) (2024)
finding: Feeds question and concept text to a pretrained encoder (BERT family) instead of only IDs. Cold start improves; on the large dataset LKT is about equal to DKT; on the small dataset DKT-type models win.
numbers: DBE-KT22 (1,361 students, 98 KCs): AKT best AUC 0.7984, DKVMN 0.7831, DKT 0.7633; LKT encoders about 0.69 to 0.76. XES3G5M-T (18,066 students, 865 KCs): DKT 0.8480, DKVMN 0.8513, LKT encoders about 0.825 to 0.851. Zero-shot: LKT pretrained on DBE-KT22 beat DKT on XES3G5M-T (DKT scored as 0.5).
limits: Text says LKT beats DKT on the big set, but the table shows near ties. Table extraction was partly garbled. Encoder models, not chat LLMs.
agent_relevance: Question text carries signal about difficulty and concept, so a text-reading model starts ahead on new items. That is the one clearly new gain: no cold start.

source: LLM-KT (2025) Aligning LLMs with knowledge tracing using a plug-and-play instruction
finding: Plug-in sequence and context adapters let a fine-tuned LLM read both the history and the item text. Reports best results on four datasets against about 20 baselines. Raw LLMs are poor at long interaction sequences.
numbers: Removing question information cuts AUC 3.08 points on Assist2009 (0.8291 vs 0.7983). Best encoder average AUC 0.8581 (ACC 0.7865); BERT-based 0.8443; LLaMA2-based lowest at 0.8116 on one dataset. GPT-4o given the long text history predicted badly.
quote: LLMs are not good at learning the sequence information or long context directly.
limits: Authors' own comparison; gains over tuned DKT/AKT are a few AUC points. Tables read from extracted text.
agent_relevance: LLMs read the item well but track the learner badly unless a trained sequence module holds the state. Matches our rule: code keeps state, the model fills slots (section 1).

source: CLST (2024) Cold-start mitigation in knowledge tracing by aligning a generative language model
finding: Fine-tunes a generative language model on interaction histories written as text. With only 8 to 64 training students it beats BKT, IRT, PFA and deep baselines on five datasets.
numbers: AUC gain over second best: up to 24.52%, 14.66%, 12.31%, 8.71% with 8, 16, 32, 64 students. By dataset: up to 13.69% NIPS34, 5.62% Algebra05, 24.52% Assist09, 9.62% Classting Social Studies, 11.82% Classting Science.
limits: Gains are largest at tiny training size and shrink as data grows. 'Up to' figures are best cases.
agent_relevance: Pretrained world knowledge helps most when data is scarce, which is our agent's situation with one learner or one task.

source: CIKT (2025) Collaborative and iterative knowledge tracing with LLMs
finding: An LLM Analyst writes a readable student profile; a Predictor forecasts the next answer; both are refined in turns. Beats classic KT on ASSIST2009, ASSIST2012 and Eedi while explaining itself. Direct GPT-4o and DeepSeek-R1 prompting is clearly worse.
numbers: Eedi: GPT-4o ACC 0.719; best CIKT about 0.770 to 0.777 ACC (+6.00% over best baseline; +7.13% on histories over 15 steps). ASSIST2009 ACC about 0.775 (CIKT-Llama3.1-8B) vs 0.743 for DKVMN. ASSIST2012 about 0.774 to 0.780. ACC gains +3.7 to +4.5% on the ASSIST sets.
limits: Table extraction was partly garbled; columns could not be fully aligned. 7B to 8B models were fine-tuned. Strongest baselines are older KT models.
agent_relevance: A readable profile plus a separate predictor beats one prompt. Supports splitting 'state summary' and 'next action' into separate calls, with code between them.

source: Systematic review (2024) Knowledge tracing and large language models in education
finding: Reviews how LLMs help KT: cold start, text features, explanation. Notes models still depend on structured, limited datasets.
numbers: No performance numbers; only the abstract listing was seen.
limits: Abstract level only.
agent_relevance: Use as a map of the LLM-KT literature, not for figures.

source: Kestin, Miller, Klales, Milbourne & Ponti (2025) AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning
finding: Crossover RCT in a Harvard physics course. A GPT-4 tutor with expert-written, question-specific prompts and step-by-step guidance beat an active-learning lesson on post-test and used less time. It was built on ITS design rules, not free chat.
numbers: N=194 students. Post-test median 4.5 (AI, n=142 lessons) vs 3.5 (active, n=174); pre-test median 2.75. Rank-sum z=-5.6, p<10^-8. Effect size 0.63 (linear regression), 0.73 or more (quantile regression). Median time on task 49 min vs 60 min class. Engagement 4.1 vs 3.6; motivation 3.4 vs 3.1.
quote: students learn significantly more in less time
limits: One course, one topic pair, short-term post-test only, no retention test. Ceiling effect in the AI group. Authors say expert-written solutions in the prompt were needed because the raw model errs.
agent_relevance: Giving the model a verified solution and a stepwise script made it work. Same rule as G2/G3: ground the tutor in a checked answer.

source: Kestin et al. (2025) time on task
finding: Time on task did not correlate with post-test score. 70% of the AI group used under 60 minutes.
numbers: 70% under 60 min, 30% over; median 49 min; no correlation of time with post-score.
limits: Self-paced home use; volunteer selection possible.
agent_relevance: Efficiency (same result in less time) was also the gain in older tutor work, so track steps used, not only accuracy.

source: Bastani et al. (2025) Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning
finding: Field RCT in a high school with GPT-4 tutors. Free access (GPT Base) raised practice scores but lowered later exam scores. A guarded tutor (GPT Tutor: given the solution, told not to reveal it, given common mistakes) removed the harm but added no gain.
numbers: Nearly 1,000 students, about fifty classes, four 90-minute sessions. Practice score +48% (GPT Base), +127% (GPT Tutor). Exam without AI -17% for GPT Base; GPT Tutor about zero. GPT Base answered practice problems correctly 51% of the time (42% logic errors, 8% arithmetic; 57 problems asked 10 times).
quote: students often use GPT Base as a crutch
limits: One school, no delayed test beyond the sessions. A correction notice exists for the PNAS paper. Students did not notice their own skill loss.
agent_relevance: An answer-giving helper hides skill loss; a tutor must withhold and check. The helper's own 49% error rate matters when it also judges.

source: Wang, Ribeiro, Robinson, Loeb & Demszky (2024, rev. 2026) Tutor CoPilot
finding: RCT of an LLM that suggests moves to human tutors in real time. Students of tutors with the tool were more likely to master topics, most for weaker tutors.
numbers: 700+ tutors, 1,000+ students. +4 percentage points topic mastery (p<.01); exit-ticket pass 62% to 66%; +9 points for lower-rated tutors; about $20 per tutor per year; 350,000+ messages analysed (more probing questions, less generic praise).
limits: Outcome is exit-ticket mastery, not a standardized test. A human stays in the loop, so it is not a pure AI tutor.
agent_relevance: Human-AI split works: the model drafts moves, an outer check decides. Gains concentrate where the base skill is weakest.

source: Pardos & Bhandari (2023) Learning gain differences between ChatGPT and human tutor generated algebra hints
finding: First learning-gain test of ChatGPT hints inside an adaptive tutor (OATutor). 70% of ChatGPT hints passed manual quality checks. Both hint types gave positive gains, but only human-written hints gave statistically significant gains.
numbers: 77 participants (Mechanical Turk), 2x2 design: Elementary vs Intermediate Algebra, human vs ChatGPT hints. Elementary control N=19, gain 24.63%; Elementary ChatGPT N=21. Human vs ChatGPT differences p=0.038 and p=0.0029 in the two topics. Intermediate ChatGPT group near ceiling at pre-test.
limits: Small N, online workers, one session, early-2023 model. Not repeated with newer models.
agent_relevance: About 30% of raw model hints failed a check, so unreviewed model output into a tutor needs a gate.

source: Kulik & Fletcher (2016) Effectiveness of intelligent tutoring systems: a meta-analytic review
finding: Meta-analysis of 50 controlled evaluations. Mostly positive but varied. Effects were larger on locally built tests than on standardized tests, and few studies were in K-12.
numbers: From the secondary review PMC12078640 (opened): 50 controlled assessments; only three in school settings, no real K-12 gain found. Median effect about 0.66 SD is from memory.
limits: Secondary description only. Developer-run studies and publication bias are known issues.
agent_relevance: Report gains on standardized or held-out checks, not self-made ones (G3).

source: Pane, McCaffrey, Slaughter, Steele & Ikemoto (2014) Effectiveness of Cognitive Tutor Algebra I at scale
finding: Large randomized trial of Cognitive Tutor Algebra I across many schools. Effect was near zero in year 1 and positive in year 2 for high schools.
numbers: From memory: about 0.20 SD in year 2 high school; near zero in year 1; middle school not significant. The review PMC12078640 (opened) confirms only that it was a large RCT of CTAI.
limits: Exact N, schools and confidence intervals not checked; RAND PDF and journal page returned errors.
agent_relevance: Real-world scale cut lab-size effects a lot and needed time for teachers to adapt. Expect the same when a scaffold leaves the tasks it was tuned on.

source: VanLehn (2011) The relative effectiveness of human tutoring, intelligent tutoring systems, and other tutoring systems
finding: Review: step-based ITS effects near human tutoring; answer-based computer help much smaller. Grain size of feedback (answer, step, substep) tracks effect size.
numbers: From memory: human tutoring d=0.79, step-based ITS d=0.76, substep-based d=0.40, answer-based d=0.31 vs no tutoring. Not verified this session.
limits: Page blocked; numbers from memory. Many studies small and author-built.
agent_relevance: Step-level feedback is the key ingredient. Mirrors our checks after every operator step.

source: Schwonke, Renkl, Krieg, Wittwer, Aleven & Salden (2009) The worked-example effect: not an artefact of lousy control conditions
finding: Added faded worked examples to a Cognitive Tutor (geometry). Learning time fell while procedural scores held and conceptual understanding rose.
numbers: From memory: about 25% less learning time at equal procedural scores in the field study; conceptual gains higher. N and p-values not verified.
limits: This is the named key work, but the primary text was not available. Details from memory.
agent_relevance: Fading support as mastery grows links knowledge tracing to worked examples (subfield 01) and expertise reversal (02).

source: Anderson (1993) Rules of the Mind; ACT-R skill theory
finding: Theory behind cognitive tutors: skills are production rules compiled from declarative knowledge. Practice strengthens rules, and a tutor can model-trace each step.
numbers: Power-law speedup with practice at rule level; no figures checked this session.
limits: Background only, not opened.
agent_relevance: Rule-level learning curves suggest tracking success per operator, not one global score.

source: Baker, Corbett & Aleven (2008); Pardos & Heffernan (2010); Yudelson et al. (2013) BKT extensions
finding: A line of BKT fixes: slip and guess per item or context, per-student learning rate and prior, item difficulty. Each lifted AUC a little.
numbers: Only a quoted figure was seen: Pardos & Heffernan best BKT AUC 0.69 on Assistments under per-skill averaging (via Khajah 2016). Other numbers unverified.
limits: Papers not opened.
agent_relevance: Parameters that vary by item and learner are the cheap upgrade over one global rate.
